A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same stochastic-policy learning project and presidential conjoint application despite the changed title and extensive revision. All 57 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original Monte Carlo simulations and analyses of presidential conjoint data and historical candidate profiles in Sections 3–4 and the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original simulations and presidential analyses and adds Max-AMCE comparisons, nonlinear-misspecification experiments, and neural-model results in Section 4 and Appendices B–C.

M1.justification: V3 adds an evaluated Bayesian Transformer outcome model with shared encoders and antisymmetrized pairwise interactions, plus implicit differentiation as an alternative to unrolling optimization. It reformulates institutional payoffs through nominee distributions and removes v1's one-step weighting estimator. The central factored-policy, regularized two-step approach remains.

E1.justification: The presidential dataset, historical candidates, and basic average-case and adversarial simulation tasks remain. V3 adds nonlinear outcome-surface scenarios for testing model misspecification, but introduces no new real-world dataset or population.

E2.justification: V3 Figure 4 adds an evaluated Max-AMCE baseline that deterministically selects each factor's estimated main-effect maximizer. V1 discusses AMCEs and presents marginal-means comparisons, but does not evaluate this combined policy in the corresponding synthetic experiment.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a GLM-versus-Transformer evaluation across misspecification magnitudes 0, 0.1, and 0.5, and evaluates both models in the presidential application. Appendix B.3 describes the adversarial policy target as pre-primary selection, whereas v1 Section 3.3 describes resulting nominees. The original sample-size, dimension, and party-share grids remain; these reported revisions do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantial outcome-model misspecification analyses, disaggregating value and policy recovery by model, nonlinearity, and dimensionality in Tables 2–3. It removes v1's one-step estimator reliability analysis, conservative variance-bound coverage experiment, and several application diagnostics. The two-step uncertainty checks and covariate-clustering analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Delta-method uncertainty and Monte Carlo coverage reporting already appear in v1. V3 newly specifies respondent-clustered application standard errors and posterior-based neural uncertainty propagation, while removing the ancillary one-step sandwich and conservative-bound treatments. An increase in replication counts is not established.

E6.justification: V3 adds Max-AMCE results with mean Q of 1.550 versus 0.783, adds robustness tables, and replaces the adversarial simulation curves. Candidate-likelihood rankings reverse: Democratic average/adversarial log probabilities are -17.23/-16.77 in v1 Table 1 but -16.05/-17.84 in v3's GLM Table 5; neural Table 4 also favors the average case. These are revised analyses, not established same-setting performance gains. Original average-case precision plots are largely retained.

T1.justification: V3 revises forced-choice assumptions and the baseline-eliminated closed-form derivation, and adds KL approximation bounds, exploitability results, conditional extragradient convergence guarantees, and explicit asymptotic theorems with proofs in Appendix A. V1's variance-bound derivations and one-step M-estimation theory are removed. This substantially changes the mathematical foundation.

C1.justification: V3 narrows equilibrium and inference claims to restricted policies and explicit regularity conditions. It drops v1's headline claim that adversarial strategies make observed candidate profiles more likely, retaining historical vote-share alignment as the principal application claim. Its stated contributions also expand to the developed neural and theoretical extensions.

C2.justification: V3 replaces v1's broadly guaranteed, stable Nash-equilibrium interpretation with restricted stationary points and qualifications concerning nonconvexity, boundary solutions, post-selection inference, and optimization or simulation error. It adds interpretations of model-misspecification results. Existing limitations concerning preference formation and institutional knowledge remain.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents the JAX backend, CPU/GPU support, 10,000 optimization iterations, default 64 Monte Carlo draws, and a Transformer with 64-dimensional embeddings, eight layers, and RMS normalization. The code repository and candidate-mapping examples were already supplied in v1. These disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments' implementation.

R1.justification: V3 substantially repositions the work within offline combinatorial policy learning, multiagent learning, variational approximation, and minimax optimization, adding references such as Levine, Littman, Nemirovski, Lorraine, and Wainwright–Jordan. It replaces much of v1's political-science and GAN-oriented discussion and softens the optimal-profile novelty claim from first to among the first.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological narrative, and contribution summary are extensively rewritten. V3 adds a policy-learning background and worked example, reorganizes the appendices, moves substantial application material out of the main text, and replaces the separate discussion/conclusion structure with compact limitations and an impact statement.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main text and substantially reorganizes the displays. Retained simulation plots move to the appendix; application panels are redrawn and separated by outcome model; new baseline and robustness displays and a neural architecture diagram appear. Several original AMCE, marginal-means, and candidate-level diagnostic plots disappear.

improvement.justification: V3 materially improves theoretical discipline by correcting unrestricted-equilibrium claims and specifying conditions for optimization and inference. However, its new neural robustness evidence is internally inconsistent: Table 2 reports zero-misspecification Q coverage of 0.43, while Table 3 reports corresponding dimension-specific values of 0.988, 0.882, and 0.650, which cannot yield that aggregate under the stated design. Because this unresolved conflict affects central uncertainty and model-comparison claims, the theoretical gains and empirical reporting problems do not establish a reliable overall direction.
